blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 5 (Solids and Fluid Dynamics), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What makes steel hard and lead soft?
blocks.explanation: It depends upon the structure of the material: the particular order and bonding of its atoms and molecules. Materials have specific uses depending on such properties as hardness, ductility and malleability.

book_ref.quote: It depends upon the structure, the particular order and bonding of atoms and molecules in a material.

blocks.prompt: 2 What are crystalline solids? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: Solids in which atoms and molecules have a regular arrangement; the neighbours of every molecule follow a regular pattern consistent throughout the crystal (an ordered structure). Examples: quartz, diamond (also calcite, sugar, mica).

book_ref.quote: There is, thus, an ordered structure in crystalline solids.

blocks.prompt: 3 Why does a crystalline solid have a definite melting point?
blocks.explanation: Its atoms vibrate about fixed points with amplitude increasing with temperature. Cohesive forces keep the long-range order until, at a certain temperature, the vibrations become so great that the structure suddenly breaks up. So the change from order (solid) to disorder (liquid) is abrupt, at a definite temperature.

book_ref.quote: For every crystal, however, there is a temperature at which the vibrations become greater that the structure suddenly breaks up

blocks.prompt: 4 Why are amorphous solids also called glassy solids?
blocks.explanation: Because they behave like ordinary glass: glass has no regular arrangement of molecules and on heating it gradually softens into a paste-like state before becoming a very viscous liquid (at almost 800 °C). Such solids have no definite melting point.

book_ref.quote: Thus, amorphous solids are also called glassy solids.

blocks.prompt: 5 Differentiate between crystalline and amorphous solids.
blocks.explanation: Crystalline solids are ordered and melt sharply; amorphous solids are disordered and soften gradually.

book_ref.quote: in amorphous solids there is no regular arrangement of molecules like that in crystalline solids

rows: Regular arrangement of atoms and molecules (long-range order).
No regular arrangement; like a liquid with its disorder frozen in.
Definite melting point; melting is abrupt.
No definite melting point; soften gradually.
Examples: quartz, calcite, sugar, mica, diamond.
Examples: glass, plastic, fused silica.

blocks.prompt: 6 What are polymeric solids? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: Polymers are solids whose structure is intermediate between order and disorder (partially or poorly crystalline). They are formed by polymerization, in which simple molecules combine into massive long-chain molecules. Examples: polythene, nylon (also polystyrene, natural rubber).

book_ref.quote: They can be classified as partially or poorly crystalline solids.

blocks.prompt: 7 Why are polymers useful as light but strong materials?
blocks.explanation: Polymers have rather low specific gravity compared with even the lightest metals, yet they show a good strength to weight ratio.

book_ref.quote: and yet exhibit good strength to weight ratio

blocks.prompt: 8 What is deformation? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Deformation is a change in shape, length or volume produced when a body is subjected to an external force. Example: squeezing a soft rubber ball changes its shape; stretching a rubber string increases its length.

book_ref.quote: From these examples, it is concluded that deformation

blocks.prompt: 9 Define elasticity. Explain it in terms of atoms.
blocks.explanation: Elasticity is the ability of a body to return to its original shape. An external force displaces atoms from their equilibrium positions (the body is under stress); when the force is removed, the atoms return to equilibrium and the body regains its shape, provided the force was not too great.

book_ref.quote: After the removal of external force, the atoms return to their equilibrium position

blocks.prompt: 10 Define stress and write its SI unit.
blocks.explanation: Stress is the force applied per unit area to produce a change in shape, volume or length: σ = F/A. Its SI unit is N m⁻², named pascal (Pa).

book_ref.quote: The SI unit of stress (σ) is newton per square meter (N m⁻²)

blocks.prompt: 11 Name the three kinds of stress according to the change they produce.
blocks.explanation: Tensile stress changes length; volume stress changes volume; shear stress changes shape.

book_ref.quote: Stress may cause a change in length, volume and shape.

blocks.prompt: 12 Define strain. Why does it have no unit?
blocks.explanation: Strain is a measure of the deformation of a solid under stress; in one dimension it is the fractional change in length, ε = ΔL/L₀. It is a ratio of two lengths, so it is dimensionless and has no unit.

book_ref.quote: In the case of deformation in one dimension, strain is defined as the fractional change in length.

blocks.prompt: 13 Differentiate between tensile strain and compressive strain.
blocks.explanation: The difference is in the stress that produces the strain.

book_ref.quote: If strain ε is due to tensile stress σ, it is called tensile strain

rows: Produced by a tensile (stretching) stress.
Produced by a compressive stress.
The length increases (ΔL is an increase).
The length decreases (ΔL is a decrease).
ε = ΔL/L₀, no unit.
ε = ΔL/L₀, no unit.

blocks.prompt: 14 Define shear strain. How is it related to the angle θ?
blocks.explanation: If two opposite faces of a body are a distance y apart and one face slides through Δx under shear stress, the shear strain is γ = Δx/y = tan θ. For a small angle θ in radian, tan θ ≅ θ, so γ = θ.

book_ref.quote: then shear strain is produced which is is given by

blocks.prompt: 15 What is volumetric strain?
blocks.explanation: When an applied stress changes the volume of a body, the change in volume per unit volume, ΔV/V₀, is the volumetric strain. It has no unit.

book_ref.quote: the change in volume per unit volume is known as volumetric strain

blocks.prompt: 16 Define Young's modulus and give its SI unit.
blocks.explanation: Young's modulus is the stress applied per unit strain: Y = tensile stress / tensile strain = (F/A)/(ΔL/L₀). Its unit is the same as that of stress, N m⁻² or Pa, because strain has no unit.

book_ref.quote: It has the same unit as that of stress i.e., N m⁻² or Pa.

blocks.prompt: 17 Differentiate between tensile stress and shear stress.
blocks.explanation: They differ in the change they produce and the strain that results.

book_ref.quote: When a stress changes length, it is called the tensile stress

rows: Changes the length of a body.
Changes the shape of a body.
Produces tensile strain ε = ΔL/L₀.
Produces shear strain γ = Δx/y = tan θ.
SI unit N m⁻² (Pa).
SI unit N m⁻² (Pa).

blocks.prompt: 18 A force of 600 N acts on a wire of cross-sectional area 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². Find the stress.

book_ref.quote: Mathematically, it is expressed as:

blocks.prompt: 19 A wire 1.5 m long is stretched by 0.30 mm. Find the strain.

book_ref.quote: If ΔL is the change in length and L₀ is the original length

blocks.prompt: 20 A wire under a stress of 1.2 × 10⁸ N m⁻² shows a strain of 6.0 × 10⁻⁴. Find Young's modulus.
blocks.explanation: Y = stress/strain = 1.2 × 10⁸ / 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻².

book_ref.quote: The stress applied per unit strain is called Young's modulus

blocks.prompt: 21 The top face of a block 10 cm thick slides 1.0 mm relative to the bottom under a shear stress. Find the shear strain and the angle θ.
blocks.explanation: γ = Δx/y = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m / 0.10 m = 0.010. For a small angle, θ ≅ tan θ = 0.010 rad.

book_ref.quote: However, for small value of angle θ, measured in radian tanθ ≅ θ, so that

blocks.prompt: 22 Using Table 5.1, which is stiffer under tension, steel or aluminium? Give the reason.
blocks.explanation: Steel. Its Young's modulus is 200 × 10⁹ N m⁻² against 70 × 10⁹ N m⁻² for aluminium, so the same stress produces a smaller strain in steel (strain = stress/Y).

book_ref.quote: Table 5.1: Elastic constants for some materials

blocks.text: 5.4 Determination of Young's modulus of a wire

blocks.prompt: 23 Why are two identical wires used in Searle's apparatus?
blocks.explanation: Searle's apparatus has a reference (auxiliary) wire and a test wire of equal length, same material and same diameter, hanging from a rigid support. The reference wire carries a constant weight; only the extension of the test wire relative to it is measured with the micrometer and spirit level.

book_ref.quote: It consists of two wires, auxiliary or reference wire and test wire

blocks.prompt: 24 Why is the diameter of the test wire measured at several points in Searle's experiment?
blocks.explanation: The diameter is measured with a screw gauge at several different points along the wire and the average is taken, so that the area A = πr² used in stress = mg/πr² is accurate.

book_ref.quote: The diameter should be measured at several different points along the wire and take average.

blocks.prompt: 25 How is Young's modulus found from the graph in Searle's experiment?
blocks.explanation: Stress (mg/πr²) and strain (ΔL/L₀) are found for several loads and plotted on a stress-strain graph. It should be a straight line; its slope equals the Young's modulus of the wire.

book_ref.quote: Plot the above values on stress strain graph, it should be straight line.

blocks.text: 5.5 Elastic deformation, plastic deformation and elastic limit

blocks.prompt: 26 Differentiate between proportional limit and elastic limit.
blocks.explanation: Both are points on the stress-strain curve of a ductile material.

book_ref.quote: From A to B, stress and strain are not proportional.

rows: Point A on the stress-strain curve.
Point B (yield point) on the curve.
Greatest stress with stress still proportional to strain (Hooke's law obeyed in OA).
Greatest stress up to which the material still returns to its original length (elastic region OB).
Denoted σₚ.
Denoted σₑ.

blocks.prompt: 27 State Hooke's law. In which region of the stress-strain curve is it obeyed?
blocks.explanation: Hooke's law: the strain (deformation) is directly proportional to the stress (force or load). It is obeyed in the region OA, up to the proportional limit A.

book_ref.quote: is obeyed in the region OA

blocks.prompt: 28 What is plastic deformation?
blocks.explanation: If the stress is increased beyond the yield stress (elastic limit), the specimen is permanently changed and does not recover its original shape or size when the stress is removed. This behaviour is plasticity; it is the region B to C of the curve.

book_ref.quote: the specimen becomes permanently changed and does not recover its original shape

blocks.prompt: 29 Define ultimate tensile strength (UTS).
blocks.explanation: UTS σᵤ is the maximum stress that a material can withstand (point C on the stress-strain curve); it is regarded as the nominal strength of the material. Beyond C the material breaks at D (fracture stress σf).

book_ref.quote: can be regarded as the nominal strength of the material

blocks.prompt: 30 Differentiate between ductile and brittle substances.
blocks.explanation: Ductile substances deform plastically before breaking; brittle ones break just after the elastic limit.

book_ref.quote: For example, Lead, copper and wrought iron are ductile substances.

rows: Undergo plastic deformation until they break.
Break just after the elastic limit is reached.
Have a large plastic region before fracture.
Have almost no plastic region.
Examples: lead, copper, wrought iron.
Examples: glass, high carbon steel, beryllium, bismuth, chromium.

blocks.prompt: 31 What is strain energy?
blocks.explanation: When a body is deformed by a force, work is done against the elastic restoring force. This work is stored in the body as potential energy, equal to the gain in P.E. of its molecules displaced from their mean positions. This stored energy is the strain energy.

book_ref.quote: It is stored in it as its potential energy

blocks.prompt: 32 Why is the work done in stretching a spring ½FΔx and not FΔx?
blocks.explanation: Within the elastic limit the extension is proportional to the force, so the force rises uniformly from zero to F. The average force is ½F, and work = average force × distance = ½FΔx (= ½kΔx², the area of triangle OPQ).

book_ref.quote: Thus, the average force that stretches the spring through Δx is 1/2F.

blocks.prompt: 33 A spring of spring constant 250 N m⁻¹ is stretched by 0.20 m. Find the energy stored in it.

book_ref.quote: Work done = Average force × Distance in the direction of the force

blocks.prompt: 34 Write strain energy per unit volume in terms of (i) stress and strain (ii) Young's modulus and strain.
blocks.explanation: Dividing ½FΔL by the volume AL: (i) U = ½ × (F/A) × (ΔL/L) = ½ × stress × strain. (ii) Putting F/A = Y(ΔL/L): U = ½Y(ΔL/L)².

book_ref.quote: Hence, the strain energy per unit volume of the material will be given by

blocks.prompt: 35 A steel wire (Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻²) is under a strain of 1.0 × 10⁻³. Find the strain energy per unit volume.

book_ref.quote: From equation of Young's Modulus (Eq. 5.6), we have

blocks.prompt: 36 What does the area under a force-extension graph represent?
blocks.explanation: It represents the work done to stretch the material (average force × extension), which equals the elastic P.E. (strain energy) stored in the material.

book_ref.quote: Work done to stretch the material is also equal to elastic P.E. stored in the material.

blocks.prompt: 37 What is upthrust? Why does an object appear to lose weight in a liquid?
blocks.explanation: Upthrust is the upward force a liquid exerts on an object kept inside it. It acts opposite to the weight, so the object seems lighter: an apparent loss of weight equal to the upthrust.

book_ref.quote: As a result, an apparent loss of weight is observed in the object.

blocks.prompt: 38 State Archimedes' principle.
blocks.explanation: When an object is totally or partially immersed in a liquid, an upthrust force acts on it equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces: Upthrust = ρgV.

book_ref.quote: Archimedes' principle states that:

blocks.prompt: 39 Why is the force on the bottom face of an immersed cylinder greater than that on its top face?
blocks.explanation: Liquid pressure increases with depth: P = ρgh. The bottom face is at the greater depth h₂, so F₂ = ρgh₂A is greater than F₁ = ρgh₁A. Their difference, ρgA(h₂ − h₁) = ρgV, is the upthrust.

book_ref.quote: This net force F on the cylinder is called the upthrust of the liquid.

blocks.prompt: 40 A body of volume 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ is completely immersed in water. Find the upthrust on it.

book_ref.quote: therefore, ρgV is the weight of the liquid displaced

blocks.prompt: 41 State the principle of floatation. When does an object float?
blocks.explanation: A floating object displaces a fluid having weight equal to its own weight. An object floats if its weight is equal to or less than the upthrust; it sinks if its weight is greater than the upthrust.

book_ref.quote: The upthrust is always equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.

blocks.prompt: 42 A block of mass 0.80 kg floats on water. Find the upthrust and the volume of water it displaces.
blocks.explanation: Floating: upthrust = weight = 0.80 × 9.8 = 7.84 N. Displaced water weighs 7.84 N, i.e. mass 0.80 kg, so V = m/ρ = 0.80/1000 = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

book_ref.quote: When an object floats in a fluid, the upthrust acting on it is equal to the weight of the object.

blocks.prompt: 43 How does a submarine dive and come up to the surface?
blocks.explanation: It has tanks that can be filled with or emptied of seawater. Filling them increases its weight; when weight exceeds the upthrust it dives. Emptying the tanks makes its weight less than the upthrust, so it rises to the surface.

book_ref.quote: A submarine can travel over as well as under water using the same principle of floatation.

blocks.prompt: 44 How is a hot-air balloon made to rise?
blocks.explanation: Its density is made less than that of the surrounding air by varying the quantity of hot air in it. When the buoyant force (upthrust of air) becomes more than its weight, it rises and floats.

book_ref.quote: This is done by varying the quantity of hot air in the balloon.

blocks.prompt: 45 What is a streamline? Why can two streamlines not cross each other?
blocks.explanation: A streamline is the smooth path followed by fluid particles in laminar flow; the tangent at any point gives the direction of flow. If two streamlines crossed, a particle there could go in either direction and the flow would no longer be steady.

book_ref.quote: The smooth path followed by fluid particles in laminar flow is called a streamline.

blocks.prompt: 46 Define steady flow.
blocks.explanation: If the overall flow pattern does not change with time, the flow is steady. Every particle follows the same flow line as the particle before it; the velocity at each point does not change with time.

book_ref.quote: In steady flow, every particle of the fluid follows the same flow line as its previous particle.

blocks.prompt: 47 Write the three conditions of an ideal fluid.
blocks.explanation: (1) Non-viscous: no frictional force between adjacent layers. (2) Incompressible: density is constant. (3) Its motion is steady.

book_ref.quote: The behaviour of the fluid which satisfies the following conditions is called ideal fluid:

blocks.prompt: 48 Show that rate of flow = Av.
blocks.explanation: In time t the fluid moves a length ℓ = vt along a pipe of area A. Volume passing = Aℓ = Avt. Rate of flow = volume/time = Avt/t = Av (unit m³ s⁻¹).

book_ref.quote: Consider a fluid flowing through a pipe of area of cross-section A

blocks.prompt: 49 Water flows at 4.0 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of area 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². Find the rate of flow in m³ s⁻¹ and in L s⁻¹.
blocks.explanation: Rate of flow = Av = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 4.0 = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹ = 2.0 L s⁻¹ (1 m³ = 1000 L).

book_ref.quote: Sometimes, it is also measured in litres per second (L s⁻¹).

blocks.prompt: 50 State the equation of continuity.
blocks.explanation: The product of cross-sectional area of the pipe and fluid speed, Av, at any point along the pipe is constant and equals the flow rate (volume per second): A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

book_ref.quote: This constant is equal to the volume flow per second of the fluid or simply the flow rate.

blocks.prompt: 51 Under what condition does A₁v₁ρ₁ = A₂v₂ρ₂ reduce to A₁v₁ = A₂v₂?
blocks.explanation: When the fluid is incompressible and the flow is steady, the density is constant (ρ₁ = ρ₂), so it cancels and A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

book_ref.quote: Since density is constant for the steady flow of incompressible fluid

blocks.prompt: 52 Water enters a pipe of diameter 4.0 cm at 1.0 m s⁻¹. Find its speed where the diameter is 2.0 cm.
blocks.explanation: A ∝ d², so A₁/A₂ = (4.0/2.0)² = 4. v₂ = A₁v₁/A₂ = 4 × 1.0 = 4.0 m s⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: Equation (5.18) states that in steady flow, the rate of flow inward is equal to the rate of flow outward.

blocks.prompt: 53 Why does a stream of water from a tap become narrower as it falls?
blocks.explanation: As the water falls, its speed increases. By the equation of continuity Av = constant, so its cross-sectional area must decrease.

book_ref.quote: As the water falls, its speed increases and so its cross sectional area decreases

blocks.prompt: 54 Why does water come out faster when the end of a rubber pipe is squeezed?
blocks.explanation: Squeezing decreases the cross-sectional area (A₂ < A₁). By A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, the velocity v₂ must increase to maintain the same flow rate.

book_ref.quote: Therefore, squeezing the rubber pipe increases the flow velocity of water.

blocks.prompt: 55 State Bernoulli's equation and its assumptions.
blocks.explanation: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. Assumptions: the fluid is incompressible, non-viscous and flows steadily.

book_ref.quote: In deriving Bernoulli's equation, we assume that the fluid is incompressible

blocks.prompt: 56 What is the meaning of each term in P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant?
blocks.explanation: P is the pressure; ½ρv² is the K.E. per unit volume; ρgh is the gravitational P.E. per unit volume. Their sum stays constant, which expresses conservation of energy for the flowing fluid.

book_ref.quote: Bernoulli's equation and is often expressed as:

blocks.prompt: 57 Water flows in a horizontal pipe. At one point P₁ = 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa and v₁ = 1.0 m s⁻¹; at another v₂ = 3.0 m s⁻¹. Find P₂.

book_ref.quote: As the fluid moves through a pipe of varying cross-section and height, the pressure will change along the pipe.

blocks.prompt: 58 How does an aeroplane wing get its lift?
blocks.explanation: The wing deflects the air so that streamlines are closer together above it than below. The air above moves faster, so by Bernoulli's equation the pressure is lower on top. The higher pressure below forces the wing upward: this is the lift.

book_ref.quote: The pressure will be lower at the top of the wing

blocks.prompt: 59 Explain the swing of a ball using Bernoulli's equation.
blocks.explanation: As described in the chapter, air moves faster over one side of the ball and slower over the other. The faster air has lower pressure and the slower air higher pressure; this pressure difference gives a sideways force (named in the book as the Magnus effect) that makes the ball curve.

book_ref.quote: known as Magnus effect which causes the ball to curves in the air

blocks.prompt: 60 How does a filter pump work?
blocks.explanation: It has a constriction in the centre, so the jet of water from the tap flows faster there. This lowers the pressure near it, so air flows in from the side tube; air and water are expelled together through the lower part.

book_ref.quote: The air and water together are expelled through the lower part of the pump.

blocks.prompt: 61 How does the carburetor of a car engine use Bernoulli's principle?
blocks.explanation: Air is drawn very fast through a Venturi duct, which creates low pressure in the duct. This draws petrol from a tiny side inlet as vapours into the air stream, feeding the correct air-petrol mixture to the cylinders.

book_ref.quote: which draws petrol vapours into the air stream

blocks.prompt: 62 How does a perfume atomizer or paint sprayer work?
blocks.explanation: Squeezing the rubber ball blows air through a tube; it rushes out of a narrow aperture at high speed, causing a fall of pressure over the dipped tube. Atmospheric pressure then pushes the liquid up the tube into the air stream.

book_ref.quote: This effect is used in perfume bottles and paint sprayers.

blocks.prompt: 63 Why is the ρgh term dropped in deriving the Venturi relation?
blocks.explanation: The venturi pipe is placed horizontally, so the average potential energy (height) is the same at both places. The ρgh terms on both sides are equal and cancel, leaving P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂².

book_ref.quote: As the pipe is placed horizontally, therefore, we consider that average potential energy is the same at both places

blocks.prompt: 64 In a venturi meter carrying water, the speed in the narrow part is 5.0 m s⁻¹. Find P₁ − P₂ using the Venturi relation.

book_ref.quote: Thus, the speed of the fluid is very slow in wider portion of the pipe

blocks.prompt: 65 State Torricelli's theorem. Why is the speed of the top surface taken as zero?
blocks.explanation: The speed of efflux equals the velocity gained by the fluid in falling through (h₁ − h₂) under gravity: v = √(2g(h₁ − h₂)). The orifices are so small that the efflux speed is much larger than the speed of the top surface, so v₁ ≈ 0.

book_ref.quote: We can therefore, take v₁ as approximately zero.

blocks.prompt: 66 Water stands 0.80 m above a small hole in a tank. Find the speed of efflux.
blocks.explanation: v = √(2g(h₁ − h₂)) = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.80) = √15.7 = 3.96 ≈ 4.0 m s⁻¹ (viscous losses would reduce it a little in practice).

book_ref.quote: In practice, viscous-energy losses would alter the result to some extent.

blocks.prompt: 67 What does the coefficient of viscosity tell us? Which has the larger value, honey or water?
blocks.explanation: It (η) tells how much force is needed to slide one layer of a liquid over another, i.e. the frictional effect between layers. Honey does not flow easily, so its η is larger; water flows easily and has a small η.

book_ref.quote: Substances which flow easily, like water, have small coefficient of viscosities.

blocks.prompt: 68 What is drag force? How does it depend on speed?
blocks.explanation: A retarding force on an object moving through a fluid is the drag force. It increases as the speed of the object increases; even the small viscosity of air gives a large drag on a fast car.

book_ref.quote: Even the small viscosity of the air causes a large retarding force on a car as it travels at high speed.

blocks.prompt: 69 State Stokes' law. When is it valid?
blocks.explanation: The drag force on a sphere of radius r moving slowly with speed v through a fluid of viscosity η is F = 6πηrv. It holds for slow motion; at high speeds the force is no longer simply proportional to speed.

book_ref.quote: However, the case of a sphere moving through a fluid is of great importance.

blocks.prompt: 70 A sphere of radius 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m moves through air (η = 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ N s m⁻²) at 1.0 m s⁻¹. Find the drag force by Stokes' law.

book_ref.quote: Since liquids and gases have non zero viscosity, therefore, a force is required

blocks.prompt: 71 Why does a tall chimney exposed to air currents work best?
blocks.explanation: Air currents moving across the top of a tall chimney reduce the pressure there. The higher pressure below then forces the smoke to flow upward.

book_ref.quote: A chimney works best when it is tall and exposed to air currents, which reduces

blocks.prompt: 72 What is terminal velocity?
blocks.explanation: As a falling droplet speeds up, the upward drag increases until it equals the weight. The net force (weight − drag) is then zero and the droplet falls with a constant speed, called terminal velocity: vₜ = 2gr²ρ/9η.

book_ref.quote: the drag force eventually approaches the weight in the magnitude

blocks.prompt: 73 Why does a fog droplet fall more slowly than a raindrop?
blocks.explanation: Terminal velocity vₜ = 2gr²ρ/9η is proportional to r². A fog droplet has a much smaller radius, so its terminal velocity is much smaller.

book_ref.quote: The droplet accelerates rapidly under the over powering force of gravity

blocks.prompt: 74 Find the terminal velocity of a water droplet of radius 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m falling through air (η = 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹).

book_ref.quote: Given that η for air = 19 x 10⁻⁶ kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ and density of water ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³.

blocks.prompt: 75 How does a parachute help a person land safely?
blocks.explanation: Its large surface area increases air resistance (drag), which counteracts the force of gravity. The drag soon balances the weight at a small terminal speed, so the fall is slowed down.

book_ref.quote: This slows down the persons fall, allowing them to land safely.

blocks.prompt: 76 Give three differences between an ideal fluid and a real fluid.
blocks.explanation: An ideal fluid exists only in theory; real fluids exist in nature.

book_ref.quote: Ideal fluids are incompressible.

rows: Zero viscosity; non-viscous flow.
Has viscosity; viscous flow.
Incompressible; bulk modulus infinite.
Compressible; finite bulk modulus.
Not subjected to surface tension.
Surface tension applies.
Imaginary; does not exist in nature.
Exists in nature, e.g. water, petrol, honey.

blocks.prompt: 77 Why is the bulk modulus of an ideal fluid infinite?
blocks.explanation: Bulk modulus depends inversely on the volume change. An ideal fluid is incompressible, so its volume change is zero, making its bulk modulus infinite.

book_ref.quote: Bulk modulus inversely depends on the volume change.

blocks.prompt: 78 What is superfluidity?
blocks.explanation: Superfluidity is the property of a fluid having zero viscosity (frictionless flow); such a substance is a superfluid. It flows without loss of kinetic energy and forms at cryogenic temperatures, not much above absolute zero.

book_ref.quote: A substance exhibiting this property is superfluid.

blocks.prompt: 79 Write two properties of superfluids not seen in ordinary fluids.
blocks.explanation: (1) Film flow: they can climb container walls and escape. (2) When stirred they form persistent vortices, and when their container is rotated the liquid inside remains still.

book_ref.quote: When stirred, superfluids create persistent vortices, unlike regular fluids that settle.

blocks.prompt: 80 Is a superfluid also a superconductor? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. Superfluidity (zero viscosity) differs from superconductivity; for example, superfluid helium-3 and helium-4 do not conduct electricity.

book_ref.quote: It is important to note that superfluidity differs from superconductivity

blocks.prompt: 81 Name two substances other than helium-4 that show superfluidity.
blocks.explanation: Superfluid helium-3 and lithium-6 atoms (at 50 nK). Others listed: some Bose Einstein condensates, atomic rubidium-85, atomic sodium, and possibly the inside of neutron stars.

book_ref.quote: Here are other supefluidity examples:
